alt: An iterative preorder DFS walking down a chain of 8 vertices, one edge case where a recursive DFS would need one call per vertex. The explicit stack shown here never holds more than one waiting vertex, because a chain has only one unvisited neighbor to push at each step, so the mechanism that avoids Python's recursion limit is visible directly in the stack's size.

steps.caption: The stack starts with just the root. This chain is 8 vertices long, far too deep for a small recursion limit, but the stack holds one entry.
Vertex 0 is visited: visit number 1 of 8. A recursive DFS would now be 1 calls deep on its own call stack; this explicit stack still holds at most one waiting vertex.
Vertex 1 is visited: visit number 2 of 8. A recursive DFS would now be 2 calls deep on its own call stack; this explicit stack still holds at most one waiting vertex.
Vertex 2 is visited: visit number 3 of 8. A recursive DFS would now be 3 calls deep on its own call stack; this explicit stack still holds at most one waiting vertex.
Vertex 3 is visited: visit number 4 of 8. A recursive DFS would now be 4 calls deep on its own call stack; this explicit stack still holds at most one waiting vertex.
Vertex 4 is visited: visit number 5 of 8. A recursive DFS would now be 5 calls deep on its own call stack; this explicit stack still holds at most one waiting vertex.
Vertex 5 is visited: visit number 6 of 8. A recursive DFS would now be 6 calls deep on its own call stack; this explicit stack still holds at most one waiting vertex.
Vertex 6 is visited: visit number 7 of 8. A recursive DFS would now be 7 calls deep on its own call stack; this explicit stack still holds at most one waiting vertex.
Vertex 7 is visited: visit number 8 of 8. A recursive DFS would now be 8 calls deep on its own call stack; this explicit stack still holds at most one waiting vertex.
Every vertex is visited. A recursive version needed a call stack 8 frames deep to reach the far end; this loop never held more than one entry on its own stack.
